claims.text: The as-processed Mg-containing lightweight HEA is initially a single-phase metastable solid solution with no or minimal observable intermetallics.
Partial short-range ordering is present in the as-cast or as-quenched initial state.
Elevated-temperature exposure causes Mg atoms to partition rapidly out of the supersaturated solid solution.
Mg partitioning produces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich intermetallics form preferentially near grain boundaries and may also form within the matrix.
Thermally processed high-entropy alloys can evolve from solid-solution-containing states into multiphase microstructures containing intermetallic compounds.
Intermetallic precipitation depletes key passivating elements from the residual matrix.
Protective alloying elements such as Cr and Al can control corrosion and oxidation resistance through formation of protective oxide layers.
Depletion of protective elements disrupts the integrity and uniformity of the surface oxide film.
Disruption of the protective oxide increases susceptibility to aqueous corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Thermal transformation will produce new diffraction reflections or TEM contrast attributable to intermetallic phases.
After sufficient thermal soaking, passivation efficacy will decline relative to the initial metastable state.
The proposed performance decline will be manifested by increased mass loss, higher corrosion current, or increased oxide spallation.
Below approximately 400–500 °C, or at insufficient dwell time, Mg partitioning and intermetallic precipitation remain minimal.
Above approximately 400–500 °C or at longer dwell times, precipitation accelerates and corrosion and oxidation resistance decline measurably.
The cited evidence does not directly establish Mg-specific precipitation kinetics or precipitate morphologies.
